analysis.one_liner: Gives House candidates full public campaign funding if they forgo private contributions, and bans party soft money.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in three House committees in 1999 and died when the 106th Congress ended, with 47 cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: Candidates for the House could qualify for full public funding of their campaigns by collecting 1,500 small $5 contributions from voters in their state and agreeing to accept no private campaign money. The bill would have banned unregulated 'soft money' contributions to national political parties, limited party spending in races with publicly funded candidates, and required disclosure of 'issue ads' paid for by outside groups. It also gave publicly funded candidates free TV and radio time at reduced ad rates, overhauled the Federal Election Commission, and barred members from sending taxpayer-funded mass mailings during their own election years.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters get a House election system where candidates do not depend on large private donors, and candidates without personal wealth or wealthy donor networks can run competitive campaigns. All taxpayers benefit if the bill's own reasoning is right: it aims to reduce legislative outcomes shaped by big contributions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters and candidates without big-money ties

how_it_helps.text: Candidates who collect 1,500 qualifying $5 contributions from registered voters in their state can be certified for public financing covering their primary and general election, and then may accept no private contributions or spend any money beyond the public grant.
A publicly funded candidate receives additional public money when a privately funded opponent or outside groups spend against them beyond 125% of the grant, capped at 200% of the grant.
Clean money candidates get 30 minutes of free broadcast time before the primary and 75 minutes before the general election, plus the right to buy TV ads at no more than half the lowest rate.

The bill bars national party committees from raising or spending soft money outside federal limits, requires rapid disclosure of issue advertisements, mandates electronic filing of FEC reports on the Internet, and gives the FEC stronger audit and enforcement powers.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the House Election Fund through open-ended appropriations. Large donors and interests that buy influence with big contributions lose their channel; political parties lose soft money; broadcasters must donate airtime and sell ads at half price to participating candidates.

drawbacks.text: The public financing is funded by appropriations of 'such sums as are necessary,' an open-ended taxpayer cost with no fixed ceiling.

The system is voluntary: a wealthy self-funder or privately funded opponent can still outspend a clean money candidate, and the matching-fund response is capped at 200% of the public grant, so a big-spending opponent can retain an advantage.

The bill forces broadcasters to provide free airtime and half-price rates and bans members' franked mass mailings in election years, costs imposed on private broadcasters and an embattled congressional privilege; the bill itself anticipates constitutional challenges by allowing direct Supreme Court review.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public cost of financing House campaigns is real but modest compared with the scale of private money the bill would displace, and the qualifying threshold of 1,500 small contributions screens out fringe candidates. The main design weakness is that the system is voluntary and matching funds are capped, so heavy-spending opponents keep some edge; still, the disclosure, soft money, and enforcement provisions stand on their own merit even if few candidates opt in.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and parceled out to subcommittees, but none of them ever acted on it, so it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. John Tierney introduced the Clean Money, Clean Elections Act on May 6, 1999, with more than 40 original cosponsors.
The bill attracted 47 cosponsors, 46 Democrats and 1 Independent; no Republicans sponsored it.
It was referred to the House Administration, Commerce, and Government Reform committees on May 6, 1999, and then to subcommittees in mid-May.
After the subcommittee referrals in May 1999, the record shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill expired with the 106th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of both parties who finance campaigns with private contributions, the major donors and party committees that provide the money, and broadcasters, who kept charging full ad rates with no free-time requirement, were all better off because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. John Tierney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as sole sponsor.

for.name: 47 House cosponsors (46 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Pelosi, Waxman, Frank, Markey, Meehan, and Kucinich, and Independent Rep. Bernie Sanders.

against.name: Republican chairmen of the House Administration, Commerce, and Government Reform committees
against.role: Committee chairs who received the bill on referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup after referral; the bill was sent to subcommittees in May 1999 and never reported out, so it never reached the floor.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Brought no campaign finance reform bill with a full public financing option to the House floor during the 106th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 47 sponsors were Democrats or the chamber's one Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican majority chaired every committee the bill was referred to, where it stalled.

industries.industry: Large campaign donors and lobbying interests
industries.note: The bill would have let candidates replace large private contributions with public funding, cutting off the primary channel through which wealthy donors and lobbying clients gain access to House members. Its stated findings target exactly this influence.

National party committees would be barred from raising and spending soft money outside federal limits, state parties would have to fund federal election activity with regulated money, and party spending would be capped in races with publicly funded candidates. The bill did offer a modest trade: higher contribution limits for state party committees and a higher individual aggregate limit.

Stations would have to give clean money candidates free airtime in prime windows, sell them ads at up to 50% off the lowest rate, and generally could not preempt purchased candidate ads — a direct transfer of airtime value from broadcasters to campaigns.

Clean money candidates could still hire consultants with their public grant and up to $35,000 in seed money, but members' franked mass mailings would be banned in election years and seed money could not fund broadcast ads, cutting into some revenue streams tied to campaign and incumbent communications.
